title: Immune Responses in Musculoskeletal Disease
subject: Musculoskeletal System (MUSC)
author: Dr. Sharilyn Rennie

overview.intro: This chapter explains how adaptive and innate immunity injure joints, muscle, and connective tissue. It covers rheumatoid arthritis from loss of tolerance to bone erosion, the clinical and serologic features that separate it from osteoarthritis and the other connective tissue diseases, the hypersensitivity type behind each disorder, crystal and bacterial inflammation in the joint, and arthritis that follows infection or vaccination. Board questions usually give a joint pattern, a synovial fluid result, or an autoantibody and ask for the disease or the effector mechanism. If you can name the cell, antibody, or cytokine doing the damage, the clinical picture follows logically.

sections.title: Rheumatoid arthritis pathogenesis: from citrullinated peptides to bone erosion

blocks.text: Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is a chronic autoimmune synovitis that destroys cartilage and bone. It begins when genetic susceptibility meets an environmental trigger. The strongest genetic link is to HLA-DR4 and related HLA-DRB1 alleles that carry the shared epitope, a sequence in the peptide binding groove that binds citrullinated peptides with high affinity. Smoking is the best established environmental factor.

Citrullination is the key molecular event. Peptidylarginine deiminase (PAD) enzymes, released by stressed or dying cells such as those in a smoker's airway, convert arginine residues to citrulline in proteins like fibrinogen, vimentin, and type II collagen. Citrulline is neutral where arginine was positively charged, which changes how the peptide folds and fits into MHC class II. Shared epitope molecules present these altered peptides to CD4 T cells, tolerance fails, and the T cells help B cells produce anti-citrullinated protein antibodies (detected as anti-CCP) and rheumatoid factor. These antibodies often appear years before the joints swell.
Effector phase in the synovium

In the joint, Th1 and Th17 CD4 T cells activate macrophages and synovial fibroblasts. Macrophages release TNF, IL-1, and IL-6. TNF and IL-1 induce endothelial adhesion molecules that recruit more leukocytes and stimulate fibroblasts and chondrocytes to secrete matrix metalloproteinases that digest cartilage collagen and proteoglycan. The normally thin synovial lining becomes a thick, villous mass of fibroblasts, lymphocytes, plasma cells, and new vessels. This pannus spreads across the cartilage surface and invades it.

Bone loss depends on osteoclasts. Activated T cells and synovial fibroblasts express RANKL, which binds RANK on osteoclast precursors and drives their maturation, while TNF and IL-1 add to the signal. Osteoclasts resorb bone first at the joint margins, the bare areas where synovium touches bone not covered by cartilage, giving marginal erosions and periarticular osteopenia on radiographs. IL-6 travels to the liver and drives the acute phase response, raising CRP and fibrinogen (and so ESR), increasing hepcidin, and producing anemia of inflammation, fatigue, and low-grade fever. RA is therefore systemic, not only articular.

sections.title: Clinical picture of rheumatoid arthritis, contrast with osteoarthritis, and Felty syndrome

blocks.text: RA typically affects women about two to three times as often as men and begins in middle age. It produces a symmetric polyarthritis of the small joints of the hands and feet: the metacarpophalangeal (MCP), proximal interphalangeal (PIP), wrist, and metatarsophalangeal joints. The distal interphalangeal (DIP) joints are characteristically spared. Larger joints and the cervical spine are involved later, and synovitis at C1 to C2 can loosen the transverse ligament and cause atlantoaxial subluxation.

Morning stiffness lasting more than 1 hour reflects inflammation. Overnight, inflammatory fluid and mediators accumulate in the synovium and periarticular tissue while the joint is still; movement gradually disperses them. Joints are warm, boggy, and tender because the swelling is synovial tissue and effusion rather than bony overgrowth.
Why the deformities form

Chronic synovitis stretches capsules, collateral ligaments, and tendon sheaths, and pannus erodes their bony attachments. At the MCP joints the extensor tendons slip toward the ulnar side, giving ulnar deviation with volar subluxation. Damage to the finger extensor mechanism and volar plate produces swan neck deformity (PIP hyperextension with DIP flexion) or boutonniere deformity (PIP flexion with DIP hyperextension). Rheumatoid nodules form over pressure points such as the extensor forearm; histologically they show central fibrinoid necrosis surrounded by palisading epithelioid histiocytes, and they occur mainly in seropositive patients.

blocks.text: Serology supports the diagnosis. Rheumatoid factor (RF) is IgM directed against the Fc portion of IgG; it is positive in about 70 to 80% of patients with RA but also appears in Sjogren syndrome, chronic infections such as hepatitis C and endocarditis, and in healthy older adults. Anti-CCP has similar or slightly lower sensitivity but specificity of about 95%, so it is the better confirmatory test and predicts more erosive disease.
Felty syndrome

Felty syndrome is the triad of RA, splenomegaly, and neutropenia. It occurs in long-standing, seropositive, often nodular disease. Neutrophils are lost through antibody and immune complex coating with splenic removal, splenic sequestration, and suppressed granulopoiesis, so patients present with recurrent bacterial infections and leg ulcers. Some cases overlap with large granular lymphocyte expansion, which can produce the same picture.

Autoantibodies are the serologic fingerprint of a connective tissue disease. Each one reflects the self antigen to which tolerance was lost, and many also predict which organ is at risk. A sensitive test helps rule a disease out when negative; a specific test helps rule it in when positive.

The antinuclear antibody (ANA) is the screening test. It is positive in more than 95% of patients with SLE but also in many other connective tissue diseases and in a meaningful fraction of healthy people, especially older women, so a positive ANA alone diagnoses nothing. Specific antibodies are then ordered to identify the disease. Anti-dsDNA and anti-Smith both point to SLE: anti-Smith is the most specific but is found in only a minority of patients, while anti-dsDNA is more common, rises with disease activity, and correlates with lupus nephritis because DNA and anti-DNA complexes deposit in glomeruli.

blocks.text: The two forms of systemic sclerosis are separated by antibody as well as by skin extent. Anti-Scl-70 (anti-topoisomerase I) marks diffuse disease, with skin thickening proximal to the elbows and knees and on the trunk, and a high risk of interstitial lung disease. Anticentromere antibody marks limited disease, also called CREST (calcinosis, Raynaud phenomenon, esophageal dysmotility, sclerodactyly, telangiectasia), with skin change confined to the face and distal limbs and a later risk of pulmonary arterial hypertension.

Anti-U1 RNP in high titer defines mixed connective tissue disease, so the antibody and the overlap syndrome travel together. Anti-Jo-1 is the most common antisynthetase antibody in inflammatory myopathy and identifies a subset with interstitial lung disease, arthritis, fever, and rough, cracked fingertips called mechanic's hands. Anti-SSA and anti-SSB are typical of Sjogren syndrome but also occur in SLE, and RF is often positive in Sjogren syndrome as well.

blocks.title: Worked example: reading a serology panel
blocks.text: A 38-year-old woman has symmetric MCP and wrist swelling. ANA is positive at a low titer, RF is positive, anti-CCP is negative, and anti-dsDNA and anti-Smith are negative. A low-titer ANA is common in healthy women, and the specific SLE antibodies are negative, so SLE is not supported. RF is positive, but RF alone also occurs in Sjogren syndrome and chronic infection, so ask about dry eyes and mouth and consider hepatitis C. A negative anti-CCP does not exclude RA, because its sensitivity is only about 60 to 70%. Persistent symmetric small joint synovitis with a positive RF still supports RA; if anti-SSA is positive with sicca symptoms, Sjogren syndrome explains both.

blocks.predict: A pregnant woman with no symptoms has anti-SSA antibodies. Which fetal organ is at risk, and why?
blocks.explain: Maternal IgG anti-SSA crosses the placenta and injures the developing fetal AV node and conduction tissue, causing congenital heart block that can be permanent.

sections.title: Musculoskeletal features of SLE, systemic sclerosis, and mixed connective tissue disease

blocks.text: The connective tissue diseases all reach the joints, but each injures a different tissue, so the joint picture differs. Asking what the immune system is attacking (synovium, collagen and small vessels, or several targets at once) predicts whether the joint erodes, stiffens, or simply hurts.
Systemic lupus erythematosus

Joint pain or arthritis is among the most common features of SLE, present in most patients at some point. The synovitis is driven by immune complex deposition and complement activation (type III hypersensitivity), producing mild synovial inflammation without the proliferative pannus of RA. Cartilage and bone are therefore not eroded, and the radiograph stays free of erosions. With time, lax capsules, ligaments, and tendons can let the fingers drift into ulnar deviation or swan neck positions that the examiner can push back into place; this reducible, nonerosive deformity is Jaccoud arthropathy. Myalgia is common, and an inflammatory myositis occurs in a minority. Osteonecrosis, especially of the femoral head, is more frequent in SLE, linked to glucocorticoid exposure, vasculitis, and antiphospholipid antibodies.
Systemic sclerosis

Systemic sclerosis (scleroderma) combines small vessel injury, autoimmunity, and fibrosis. Endothelial damage and intimal proliferation narrow digital arteries, and activated fibroblasts, stimulated largely by TGF-beta, deposit excess collagen in skin and deeper tissues. Raynaud phenomenon is usually the first sign: cold or emotion triggers vasospasm in already narrowed vessels, so the fingers turn white (ischemia), then blue (deoxygenated blood), then red (reactive hyperemia). Chronic ischemia causes digital pitting scars, ulcers, and resorption of the terminal phalangeal tufts (acro-osteolysis).

Fibrosis of skin and tendon sheaths produces sclerodactyly, tight shiny skin that tethers the fingers, and fixed flexion contractures as the hand loses the ability to extend. In diffuse disease, fibrin and fibrosis in tendon sheaths can produce palpable tendon friction rubs, which signal more aggressive disease. Calcinosis cutis is the deposition of calcium hydroxyapatite in subcutaneous tissue, typically over fingertips and extensor surfaces, and can ulcerate and drain chalky material. Muscle can be involved by a fibrosing or inflammatory myopathy.
Mixed connective tissue disease

Mixed connective tissue disease (MCTD) is an overlap syndrome defined by high-titer anti-U1 RNP together with features of SLE, systemic sclerosis, and polymyositis. Raynaud phenomenon is nearly universal and diffusely swollen, puffy hands are common early, and patients also have inflammatory arthritis, myositis with elevated creatine kinase, and esophageal dysmotility. Severe renal and central nervous system disease are less common than in SLE, while pulmonary arterial hypertension is the leading cause of death. Some patients later evolve toward one defined disease.

sections.title: Hypersensitivity mechanisms in joint, nerve, and muscle disease

blocks.text: Hypersensitivity types are defined by the effector mechanism, not by the organ. Type I is IgE and mast cell mediated; type II is antibody bound to an antigen fixed on a cell or in tissue; type III is circulating antigen-antibody complexes that deposit and activate complement; type IV is T cell mediated injury without antibody. To classify any disease, ask what is doing the damage and where the antigen sits.

blocks.text: Type II: antibody against tissue

Acute rheumatic fever follows group A streptococcal pharyngitis by about 2 to 4 weeks. Antibodies and T cells raised against the streptococcal M protein and cell wall cross-react with self proteins in heart, joints, brain, and skin, a process called molecular mimicry. The arthritis is a migratory polyarthritis of large joints such as knees, ankles, elbows, and wrists; each joint is inflamed for days and the arthritis heals without deformity, unlike the carditis, which can scar valves.

Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome shows that type II injury can alter function without killing cells. Small cell lung cancer, the trigger in about half of patients, is a neuroendocrine tumor that expresses voltage-gated calcium channels. Antibodies raised against tumor P/Q type channels cross-react with the same channels on presynaptic motor nerve terminals and reduce calcium entry, so fewer acetylcholine quanta are released per impulse. Patients have proximal weakness, reduced reflexes, and autonomic symptoms such as dry mouth. Repeated or sustained contraction lets calcium accumulate in the terminal, so strength and reflexes briefly improve after exercise, and high-frequency nerve stimulation produces an increasing muscle response. Myasthenia gravis is also type II, but its antibodies target the postsynaptic acetylcholine receptor and weakness worsens with use.

blocks.text: Type III and type IV

In SLE, antibodies to nuclear antigens form complexes with material released from dying cells. The complexes deposit in synovium, vessel walls, and glomeruli, activate complement (lowering serum C3 and C4), and attract neutrophils, which is type III injury. In polymyositis, muscle fibers abnormally express MHC class I, and CD8 cytotoxic T cells invade the endomysium and kill nonnecrotic fibers, which is type IV injury and produces symmetric proximal weakness with high creatine kinase. Dermatomyositis differs: complement-mediated injury to capillaries causes perifascicular atrophy, with a perimysial and perivascular infiltrate rich in CD4 T cells and B cells.

blocks.predict: Lambert-Eaton syndrome begins with a tumor and involves no immune complexes. Why is it still type II hypersensitivity?
blocks.explain: The injury is caused by antibody binding an antigen fixed in tissue, the presynaptic calcium channel, and altering its function; the source of the original immunizing antigen does not change the effector mechanism.

sections.title: Innate immune activation in the joint: gout and septic arthritis

blocks.text: Gout and septic arthritis show that a joint can be destroyed without autoimmunity. In both, innate pattern recognition, cytokines, and neutrophils produce intense inflammation within hours. Neither needs prior sensitization or antigen specificity.
Gout and the NLRP3 inflammasome

Uric acid is the end product of purine metabolism in humans. Serum urate saturates at about 6.8 mg/dL at 37 °C (98.6 °F); above that level monosodium urate crystals can form, and solubility falls further at lower temperature, which helps explain why the cooler first metatarsophalangeal joint (podagra) is a classic site. Crystals can sit in a joint silently until they are shed or newly formed, then trigger an attack.

The flare needs two signals. Priming through Toll-like receptors and NF-kappa B (from free fatty acids, for example) makes macrophages transcribe pro-IL-1 beta and NLRP3. When macrophages phagocytose urate crystals, the crystals damage lysosomes and cause potassium efflux, which assembles NLRP3 with the adaptor ASC and pro-caspase-1. Active caspase-1 cleaves pro-IL-1 beta into IL-1 beta. IL-1 beta activates endothelium and induces chemokines such as IL-8, drawing in neutrophils that ingest crystals and release more mediators, so the joint becomes hot, red, and exquisitely tender. Flares are self-limited partly because neutrophil extracellular traps aggregate crystals and degrade cytokines. Aspirated fluid shows needle-shaped, negatively birefringent crystals, often inside neutrophils.

blocks.text: Septic arthritis

Bacteria reach the joint usually by hematogenous spread, less often by direct inoculation. Staphylococcus aureus is the most common cause overall, and Neisseria gonorrhoeae is an important cause in sexually active young adults. Bacterial products activate Toll-like receptors on synovial cells, releasing TNF and IL-1 and recruiting huge numbers of neutrophils. Neutrophil elastase and other proteases, metalloproteinases from IL-1 stimulated chondrocytes, and bacterial toxins strip proteoglycan from cartilage within about 2 days and then break down collagen. The tense effusion also impairs nutrient diffusion into cartilage. Because articular cartilage is avascular and has little capacity for repair, this damage is permanent within days, which makes the hot, swollen, single joint a medical emergency until infection is excluded.

blocks.title: Worked example: crystals do not exclude infection
blocks.text: A 62-year-old man with known gout has a hot right knee and a temperature of 38.6 °C (101.5 °F). Aspirate shows 85,000 WBC/uL, 92% neutrophils, and negatively birefringent needles; the Gram stain is negative. The crystals prove gout is present, but not that gout is the only process. A count above 50,000 with high neutrophil predominance and fever overlaps the septic range, a Gram stain misses many infections, and crystals and bacteria can coexist in the same joint. Because infection destroys cartilage within days, culture must exclude it before the flare is blamed on gout alone.

Some arthritis follows an infection rather than being caused by live organisms growing in the joint. The joint fluid is sterile on culture, and the inflammation reflects the host response to a recent microbe. Timing, joint pattern, and host genetics identify the cause.
Reactive arthritis

Reactive arthritis is a spondyloarthritis that develops about 1 to 4 weeks after a gastrointestinal infection with Salmonella, Shigella, Yersinia, or Campylobacter, or a genitourinary infection with Chlamydia trachomatis. It is associated with HLA-B27, an MHC class I allele. Bacterial antigens, and for Chlamydia even viable organisms that cannot be cultured, are carried to the synovium by monocytes. Proposed mechanisms include HLA-B27 presenting cross-reactive bacterial peptides to CD8 T cells and misfolding of HLA-B27 that drives IL-23 and IL-17 production; impaired clearance of the organism by HLA-B27 positive cells may also contribute.

The pattern is an asymmetric oligoarthritis of the lower limbs, often knees and ankles, with enthesitis (Achilles tendon, plantar fascia), dactylitis (sausage digits), and sometimes sacroiliitis. Extra-articular features include conjunctivitis, urethritis or cervicitis, and skin and mucosal lesions such as keratoderma blennorrhagicum. This differs from RA because inflammation centers on entheses and lower limb joints rather than on symmetric hand synovium, and RF and anti-CCP are negative.

blocks.text: Viral and postvaccine arthritis

Parvovirus B19 causes erythema infectiosum in children, but in adults, particularly women, it more often causes an acute symmetric polyarthritis of the MCP, PIP, wrist, and knee joints. Because this pattern mirrors early RA, it is a classic mimic, and RF can be transiently positive. Joint symptoms begin as specific IgM appears, consistent with immune complex formation, and usually resolve within weeks without erosion. Rubella infection produces a similar symmetric small joint arthritis in adult women around the time of the rash, through immune complexes and direct infection of synovium.

The live attenuated rubella vaccine reproduces this pattern on a smaller scale. Susceptible postpubertal women are most affected, developing arthralgia or, less often, arthritis about 1 to 3 weeks after vaccination that lasts days to weeks. Children and men rarely have joint symptoms. The replicating vaccine virus provokes the same response as natural infection.

integration.text: Immunology supplies the classification and pathology supplies the joint picture. Adaptive immunity against a specific self antigen drives RA, SLE, systemic sclerosis, and myositis, and the effector (T cell, antibody against tissue, or immune complex) determines whether synovium proliferates, immune complexes deposit, or muscle fibers are killed. Innate immunity explains gout and septic arthritis, where crystals or bacteria trigger neutrophil inflammation without antigen specificity. Microbiology links the two through molecular mimicry in rheumatic fever and antigen persistence in reactive arthritis, while biochemistry explains citrullination and urate solubility, and bone biology explains why RANKL turns synovitis into erosion.

These categories have limits. Many diseases use more than one mechanism: RA involves T cells, autoantibodies, and immune complexes, and dermatomyositis does not fit neatly into one hypersensitivity type. Autoantibodies support a diagnosis but are not diagnostic alone, since ANA and RF occur in healthy people and anti-CCP is negative in about a third of patients with RA. Synovial fluid white cell counts overlap among gout, RA, and infection, so crystals and culture, not the count, settle the question.

summary: RA begins when HLA-DR4 shared epitope molecules present citrullinated peptides, CD4 T cells break tolerance, and B cells make anti-CCP and rheumatoid factor.
TNF, IL-1, and IL-6 drive pannus and systemic inflammation; metalloproteinases degrade cartilage and RANKL-activated osteoclasts cause marginal erosions.
RA is a symmetric MCP, PIP, and wrist synovitis sparing the DIP with stiffness over 1 hour; osteoarthritis involves the DIP, worsens with use, and forms osteophytes.
Felty syndrome is RA with splenomegaly and neutropenia, causing recurrent bacterial infections.

Anti-CCP is the most specific test for RA, anti-Smith for SLE, anti-Scl-70 for diffuse and anticentromere for limited systemic sclerosis, anti-U1 RNP for MCTD, anti-Jo-1 for myositis, and anti-SSA and anti-SSB for Sjogren syndrome.
SLE arthritis is nonerosive with reducible deformity; systemic sclerosis causes Raynaud phenomenon, sclerodactyly, calcinosis, and flexion contractures.
Rheumatic fever arthritis and Lambert-Eaton syndrome are type II, SLE arthritis is type III, and polymyositis is type IV with CD8 T cells killing MHC class I positive fibers.
Urate crystals activate the NLRP3 inflammasome and caspase-1 to release IL-1 beta, which recruits neutrophils; septic arthritis destroys avascular cartilage within days.
Reactive arthritis is sterile, HLA-B27 associated, asymmetric lower limb arthritis with enthesitis 1 to 4 weeks after enteric or chlamydial infection.
Parvovirus B19 and rubella cause self-limited symmetric small joint arthritis in adult women that mimics RA; rubella vaccine causes transient arthralgia in susceptible adult women.
